lesson.title: Reading the Triangle: Decoding the Op-Amp Schematic Symbol
lesson.summary: The op-amp schematic symbol packs an enormous amount of functional information, inputs, output, and power, into one simple triangle, and learning to read it correctly is the first real step toward designing with operational amplifiers.
lesson.body:
An operational amplifier is drawn on a schematic as a triangle pointing in the direction signal flow travels, almost always left to right, with two input lines entering the flat side on the left and a single output line leaving the point on the right. This triangle shape follows the general convention used across circuit schematic symbols where amplifying or processing blocks are drawn as triangles pointing toward the output, distinguishing them at a glance from passive components like resistors and capacitors, which use their own distinct symbols entirely. What makes the op-amp symbol specifically identifiable, beyond the generic amplifier triangle, is the pair of labeled inputs: one marked with a minus sign, called the inverting input, and one marked with a plus sign, called the non-inverting input.

These two labels are not arbitrary. A signal applied to the inverting, minus, input produces an amplified output flipped in polarity, 180 degrees out of phase with the input, while a signal applied to the non-inverting, plus, input produces an output that stays in phase with the input. Real op-amp chips also need power to operate, so the symbol often includes two additional pins for the supply rails, labeled V+ and V minus, though these are sometimes omitted from simplified schematics. A classic, still widely referenced example is the 741 op-amp in its 8 pin package, where pin 2 is the inverting input, pin 3 is the non-inverting input, pin 6 is the output, pin 7 connects to the positive supply, and pin 4 connects to the negative supply, a pinout reused across many compatible op-amp parts since its introduction.

Reading the symbol becomes concrete once resistors are added around it. In the standard inverting amplifier configuration, the input signal connects through a resistor Rin to the inverting input, a feedback resistor Rf connects from the output back to that same inverting input, and the non-inverting input is tied directly to ground. This produces a voltage gain of Av = negative Rf divided by Rin, the negative sign reflecting the inverting input's polarity flipping behavior. Worked example: with Rf = 100 kilohms and Rin = 10 kilohms, the gain is Av = negative 100/10 = negative 10. Applying a 0.2 volt input, the output is Vout = Av times Vin = negative 10 times 0.2 = negative 2 volts. Checking the arithmetic, 100 divided by 10 is exactly 10, and 10 times 0.2 is exactly 2, confirming an inverted, ten times amplified output of negative 2 volts for a plus 0.2 volt input.

Because the same triangular symbol is reused for every op-amp application, comparator, buffer, inverting amplifier, non-inverting amplifier, integrator, the symbol alone never tells you what the circuit does. What determines the function is entirely the external components wired around the two inputs and the feedback path, which is precisely why learning to trace where the feedback resistor connects, whether it returns to the inverting or non-inverting input, and what impedance sits in the input path, matters so much more than simply recognizing the triangle shape on sight. The symbol is the constant, the wiring around it is the variable that determines behavior.

Learning to read this symbol fluently pays off once real schematics get more complex, since multi op-amp circuits, active filters, instrumentation amplifiers, and oscillators all reuse this same triangle repeatedly, and being able to instantly identify which input is inverting, which is non-inverting, and where feedback closes the loop is one of the most important schematic reading skills in analog design.
